data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories smuggles induction back into Popper's system, rendering his rejection of induction inconsistent with his methodology of science.","counterconditions":[{"case":"If Popper explicitly accepts that his method relies on a non-justified, biological faith in regularity.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the definition of 'severe test' inherently contains an inductive premise about background knowledge.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If the distinction between 'acting on' a theory and 'believing' a theory collapses under scrutiny.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The 'Pragmatic Vindication' critique: To prefer Theory A over Theory B because A has survived tests while B has not (or A has survived more severe tests) is to assume that the property of 'having survived tests' is a reliable indicator of future performance or truth. This assumption is itself an inductive principle (the uniformity of nature regarding testability). Without this inductive bridge, the fact that a theory worked yesterday provides zero logical force for expecting it to work tomorrow. Thus, Popper's 'critical preference' is induction by another name.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
